summary: Procedural KS3 chemistry (ages 11–13) on separating mixtures: selecting and running filtration, crystallisation/evaporation, distillation and chromatography by reasoning from the relevant property difference (particle size/insolubility, solubility, boiling point, differential travel up paper). The core skill is matching technique to BOTH the exploited property AND which component is wanted, and sequencing steps for multi-component mixtures. An interactive separation lab is the primary proposal; labelled apparatus references, matching/sequencing/chromatogram tasks, and real hands-on practicals (with appropriate safety) are preserved as complements.
misconceptions: Filtration can separate a dissolved solid from its solution (it passes through).
Distillation destroys or leaves the liquid behind, rather than collecting it pure after condensing.
In distillation the collected liquid is the impurity rather than the purified solvent.
Chromatography colours are added by the paper rather than separated from the mixture.
One separation step always suffices, ignoring the need for a sequence.

activities.title: Separation lab: choose, run, and check the technique
steps: Work from a mixture bank: muddy/sandy water, salty water, rock salt, a spot of black felt-tip ink.
For each mixture, first state the property difference between its components (insoluble solid? dissolved solid? liquids of different boiling point? different coloured dyes?) BEFORE choosing a method.
Choose and set up one of four stations — filtration, crystallisation/evaporation, distillation, chromatography — and run it.

At filtration: pour muddy water through filter paper. Watch a clearer filtrate drip through while insoluble mud/sand stays on the paper. Note that very fine particles can leave it slightly cloudy and that anything dissolved passes through, so the filtrate is not pure water.
At crystallisation/evaporation: heat salty water and watch white salt left behind as the water leaves.

At distillation: watch the solvent boil up, travel into the cooled condenser, turn back to liquid and drip out as pure liquid while the salt stays in the flask — trace the one flow heat→evaporate→condense→collect.

At chromatography: place an ink spot on a pencil start line near the bottom of the paper. Stand the paper in solvent kept BELOW the spot so the dye climbs the paper rather than washing straight into the solvent. Watch whether the black dot climbs and splits into separate coloured spots; many black inks do, but not all. Count the spots to give the minimum number of dyes present.

Tackle a multi-component mixture (e.g. rock salt treated as salt + insoluble rock/sand: dissolve in water, filter off the insoluble rock/sand, then recover the salt) that requires an ordered sequence of techniques.

Deliberately try a mismatched technique (e.g. filtering salty water). Show that it fails by evaporating a few drops of the filtrate: white salt is left behind, so the salt went through the paper. Then revise the choice using the property.
activities.insight: Each technique exploits a specific property difference, so the method must be selected from the mixture's properties and from which component you want to keep — not recalled from a past practical. Distillation keeps the liquid (condensed and collected pure); evaporation/crystallisation keeps the solid. Chromatography shows at least how many substances are present.

activities.title: Labelled apparatus reference with 'what it separates and why'
steps: Study a labelled diagram of each apparatus, focusing on the distillation setup: heat source, flask, vapour path, cooled condenser, and collected distillate.
For each setup, reveal a short note stating what it separates and which property it exploits.
Trace on the distillation diagram where the vapour cools and where the pure liquid is collected.
Examine a chromatography diagram showing the solvent front and spots at different heights, with the start line (and ink spot) above the solvent level.
activities.insight: Learners build an accurate mental picture of each apparatus and can name the property each technique relies on, with distillation understood as a connected evaporate-then-condense flow.

activities.title: Match, sequence, and read a chromatogram
steps: Match each described mixture to the technique that exploits the right property difference.
Put the steps of a multi-technique separation (e.g. salt + insoluble sand in water) into a working order.

Read a given chromatogram: state how many components are present and which travelled furthest, and, where distances are provided, compute or compare Rf values (distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent front).
Explain in one line why filtration removes sand from water but not dissolved salt.
activities.insight: Learners consolidate technique selection, step sequencing, and chromatogram interpretation, including that the number of spots shows the minimum number of substances.

activities.title: Real separation practicals (hands-on complement)
steps: Carry out a real filtration of muddy water and inspect the filtrate.

Set up a real distillation of salty water and collect the distillate. Test whether the distillate is free of salt by evaporating a few drops on a clean watch glass and checking for any white residue. Appearance can't show this, because salty water also looks clear, and salt left in the flask says nothing about the distillate. Never taste substances in the lab.
Run paper chromatography on a felt-tip ink spot, keeping the solvent level below the spot, and count the separated colours.
Where safe apparatus and supervision allow, assemble the distillation apparatus so the physical connections (flask, condenser, collection vessel) are handled directly.
activities.insight: Real practicals give direct experience of assembling apparatus, handling real materials, and observing genuine outcomes, reinforcing that method choice is justified by what actually separates.

checkQuestion: Set out three labelled mixtures and the full kit (filter funnel + paper, distillation setup, evaporating basin, chromatography paper + solvent): (1) muddy water, (2) salty water where the teacher wants the WATER back as drinkable liquid, (3) a spot of black felt-tip ink. Say: 'For each one, choose a separation method, set it up, and tell me what you'll collect.' Watch the choices and the setups — don't name the techniques for them.
checkAnswer: (1) Muddy water → FILTRATION: mud (insoluble) stays on the paper, clear water passes through. (2) Salty water, wanting the water → (simple) DISTILLATION: boil, condense and collect the pure water; salt stays behind (evaporation/crystallisation would keep the salt and lose the water). (3) Ink → CHROMATOGRAPHY: the dyes travel up the paper at different rates and separate into spots. The critical judgements are matching technique to the property exploited AND to which component is wanted.
